reader.title: Reported lynching of Ferguson at Charleston, Massachusetts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The only report attributes Ferguson's fate to 'Judge Lynch' and says he was spared a trial and the scaffold, which implies a killing by a mob, though no act is described (A1).

A Montana editorial says 'Judge Lynch' dealt with Ferguson, charged with outraging a widow, so that he would escape trial and the hangman, which implies an extralegal killing for an alleged crime; it gives no description of the killing, the number of perpetrators, date or Ferguson's race (A1).
One secondhand editorial aside in a Montana weekly is the only report; no original dispatch or local report was found (A1).

summary.text: The reported lynching of Ferguson at Charleston, Massachusetts, is known only from an editorial paragraph in the Benton Weekly Record of Benton, Montana, on June 29, 1882, which said that "Judge Lynch" had lately dealt with a man named Ferguson charged with outraging a widow and causing her death.
The paragraph implied that Ferguson was killed but gave no date, description of the act, or race for anyone involved.
According to the Montana paper, Ferguson had been "charged with outraging a widow, causing her death, at Charleston, Mass."
The editorial said Judge Lynch had "latley paid his respects" to him, so that he would now be "relieved from the suspense of a tedious trial" and from the hangman's scaffold.
It did not say how, when or by whom he was killed, how many took part, or whether he had been in custody.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and no other account of the case was found.
The item was not a news dispatch but a passing example in an editorial on the spread of lynching, which opened, "JUDGE Lynch, with masked face and stealthy tread, is moving rapidly over the country."
The writer added that Judge Lynch "knows no North, no South, no East, no West," with victims hanging "from trees in Maryland as well as Kansas and California," a general remark not tied to Ferguson.
Its tone toward Ferguson was ironic rather than condemning, treating his escape from trial and the gallows as a relief to him.
No Massachusetts paper or wire report carrying the story was found, so the place, the date and Ferguson's race remain unconfirmed.
